item.title: Holdout Juror in Lindsay Clancy Case Says He Didn’t Doubt Her Guilt
item.description:
The lone juror who had wanted to convict Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman who was on trial this month for killing her three young children, said on Friday that he had no doubt that she was guilty.

In a statement, the holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, said that other jurors repeatedly cut him off during deliberations when he tried to propose his theories about the case. He defended himself against accusations from some of the other jurors, who said he refused to follow the law regarding reasonable doubt.

“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” Mr. Desronvil said of Ms. Clancy.

Mr. Desronvil, 48, released the statement through his lawyer, Edward Paltzik, who specializes in defamation litigation and has represented President Trump in lawsuits against CBS News and The New York Times.

Mr. Paltzik also released a statement on social media that called his client an American hero, and said they would share more information in the coming days. He declined to signal what, if any, legal actions may come from Mr. Desronvil, who received both withering criticism and outspoken support in the wake of his jury service.

The trial of Ms. Clancy ended this month with the jury deadlocked, 11 to 1, in favor of acquitting her on murder and manslaughter charges. Jurors deliberated for roughly 38 hours across seven days before the judge declared a mistrial.

Ms. Clancy had admitted to strangling her three children, in January 2023, but her lawyers had argued she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and should be absolved of criminal responsibility.

The case horrified and divided the country and prompted discussions of postpartum complications.

Prosecutors have not said whether they will retry Ms. Clancy, 36, who remains in custody in a state-run psychiatric center.

Following the mistrial, national attention turned to the jury of nine women and three men, and in particular to the holdout. The court has not revealed their identities — their names remain under seal — but several jurors have spoken publicly about their experience.

Identifying details about Mr. Desronvil began to emerge in the news media, including the fact that he had been charged, in 2021, with misdemeanor domestic violence after his then-partner said he had grabbed her throat and thrown her against a dresser. That charge was later dismissed.

Then, last year, a teenage family member asked a judge for a restraining order against Mr. Desronvil. The yearlong order expired last month, during the trial.

Mr. Desronvil was not prohibited from serving on a jury. Massachusetts law bars only people who have been convicted of a felony in the last seven years. But the charges raised questions about how Mr. Desronvil had responded when asked, on a juror form, about whether he had ever been charged with a crime, as well as whether Ms. Clancy’s lawyers had made a mistake by not trying to have him removed.

On Friday, Mr. Desronvil said in his statement that he “didn’t have any doubts” about the case.

Mr. Paltzik, his lawyer, described him on social media as a “HERO holdout” and said that he was “safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location” in rural New England. He also asked people to stop calling his client and to stay away from his home.

The lawyer also said that Mr. Desronvil “supports our amazing leader, President Donald J. Trump.” (A lawyer for Ms. Clancy previously called on Mr. Trump to pardon his client, though the president has no power to wipe away state charges.)

Mr. Paltzik had previously noted that Mr. Desronvil, who is Black, was the only nonwhite person on the jury, and said he had been “viciously attacked” in public comments by several white jurors who served with him.

In addition to representing Mr. Desronvil and Mr. Trump, Mr. Paltzik also recently began representing three young men who were friends with Nolan Wells, a Black man who died after spending time on an island with friends on July 4 in Mississippi.

The friends, who are white, had come under social media scrutiny following Mr. Wells’s death, which the authorities said was a suspected drowning but remains under investigation. Mr. Paltzik has said that the friends were unfairly defamed and has started a fund-raiser for them.

item.title: Trump Calls A.I. Fears a Hoax. Inside the White House, the Debate Is More Complex.
item.description:
President Trump made clear in the past week that he views fears that A.I. could lead to mass extinction as a “HOAX,” and that he sees opponents of data centers as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

People who have discussed the subject with Mr. Trump in private say his outbursts are rooted in worries that if the artificial intelligence boom fueling the American economy slows down, the market could crash and recession could quickly follow.

His anti-regulatory, anti-slowdown outbursts have been encouraged by a slice of Silicon Valley’s most influential voices. Chief among them has been David Sacks, the venture capitalist who interceded to weaken an executive order in May that would have required safety reviews of new A.I. models. Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia have also spoken to the president. All have advised Mr. Trump that the bigger risk is being overtaken by Chinese competitors.

But inside the administration, the debate is far more complex, and there are other voices in Mr. Trump’s ear, urging caution.

The more cautious tone inside the White House reflects a growing concern that despite the strategic challenge posed by China, a summer of A.I. surprises has raised the prospect of risks that were often dismissed a year ago as the wild talk of “doomers.”

Now, even the biggest A.I. boosters in the administration concede that A.I.-fueled hacks into infrastructure, biological threats, attacks on nuclear command-and-control systems, job losses and global financial instability seem more possible than they did before A.I. agents went rogue.

The issue of A.I. safety is expected to come to a head this weekend as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent meets in New York with his Chinese counterpart to set the agenda for Mr. Trump’s visit in Washington with President Xi Jinping of China, which starts on Wednesday. Mr. Bessent is trying to negotiate some kind of agreement between Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi that would suggest the two countries are working together on mutual A.I. safety concerns.

But already, officials say, some of the most expansive ideas being discussed among A.I. safety experts, including an agreement on safety standards and reviews of forthcoming Chinese and American A.I. models before their public release, are unlikely to be part of any initial accord.

One diplomat involved in the effort said he believed “the best we can hope for” is the creation of some kind of U.S.-China working group that might build on a Biden-era agreement with China to bar the use of artificial intelligence in decisions about the employment of nuclear weapons. But that does not begin to get at the complexity of the problem of unpredictable A.I.-driven agents, which took the industry and the government by surprise this summer.

Nor does it get to the fundamental issues surrounding imposing safeguards on frontier models. The United States could go its own way and impose mandatory reviews of the safety of new, American-generated models, but Mr. Trump and his aides believe that would effectively drive the global market to Chinese largely open-source alternatives. And because those open-source models can be modified by users — who could remove the “guardrails” meant to limit their powers — a safety review may mean little.

Mr. Trump wants to meet with the A.I. executives next week, according to company representatives. (A White House official said on Thursday that nothing was on the schedule as of now.)

If that session happens, it would presumably include some of the A.I. executives who, in recent days, have been calling for the kind of slowdown in the release of new models that Mr. Trump says he opposes.

Few expect Dario Amodei, a founder of Anthropic, to be among the invitees: His company’s products have been banned by the Pentagon, and he appeared to anger Mr. Trump by proposing last weekend a detailed plan for the industry to pace itself and bring in independent safety inspectors. Mr. Trump dismissed him, and denounced an unnamed class of “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors and Leakers” who were politicizing the debate over A.I. and undercutting American leadership.

But another Anthropic founder, Tom Brown, who raises less ire in the White House, talks to officials regularly. In recent days, Mr. Trump has also talked with Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX, both of whom endorsed Mr. Amodei’s plan to slow down, test new models for vulnerabilities and let in outside inspectors, at least in general terms.

Mr. Bessent and the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, have been increasingly concerned over the past several months that A.I. could cause massive disruptions across industries, including hacks into major financial institutions that could destabilize the world economy.

Ms. Wiles this year began organizing an informal group to think about how to deal with the risk created by new, more powerful models. Mr. Bessent is chief among the members of that informal group, an administration official said, but other experts are called in depending on the topic.

The White House pointed to Ms. Wiles’s social media post on May 6 as the foundational statement of how Mr. Trump balances the risks and opportunities of the new technology. “This administration has one goal: ensure the best and safest tech is deployed rapidly to defeat any and all threats,” she wrote at the time. She said that “the White House will continue to lead an America First effort that empowers America’s great innovators, not bureaucracy, to drive safe deployment of powerful technologies while keeping America safe.”

Asked about Mr. Trump’s accusation that A.I. risk is overblown, Elizabeth Huston, a White House spokeswoman, said that “President Trump is saying that Democrats using A.I. concern as a way to score points is a hoax, just like their claims that climate change would kill everyone in six years.”

She added that Mr. Trump had reversed the “failed approach” of the Biden administration, which she said had “stifled innovation, hurt consumers and nearly cost America its competitive edge over China.”

But at a moment when A.I. has emerged as arguably the most important long-term issue for the country’s economic health and national security, in the Trump White House there is no single person in charge of coordinating A.I. policy. Marco Rubio, in his role as national security adviser, is rarely discussed as a player on these issues. The White House eliminated the post of deputy national security adviser for cyber and emerging technologies created during the Biden administration.

And the national cyber director, a position created by Congress, has only indirect authority over artificial intelligence issues. The current director is Sean Cairncross, a former senior official at the Republican National Committee, who was light on cyber and A.I. experience before taking the post.

And there has been a purging of some technical expertise, including at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, part of the Department of Homeland Security. (The acting director of CISA said last week that the agency was hiring about 250 new employees after shedding around a thousand jobs — roughly a third of its work force — since Mr. Trump returned to the White House.)

As a result, A.I. has become the administration’s latest hot potato, with various officials dipping in and out of influence depending on the topic, or the day of the week.

Still, there are other officials, particularly in the much-shrunken National Security Council and the Energy Department, who share Mr. Amodei’s fears about charging ahead with new, more powerful models amid growing evidence that they are increasingly unpredictable.

Amid the rising turmoil over A.I., several White House staff members working on security and policy issues related to the technology have left in recent months.

The cyber director’s office, which has been heavily involved in A.I. safety debates, saw two of its top policy officials depart this summer. Sriram Krishnan, the White House’s senior policy adviser for A.I., also left. And just this week, Sihao Huang, a top A.I. policy official in the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, announced on X that he, too, was leaving — to join Anthropic.

Former administration officials said that working on A.I. policy has been a frustrating endeavor because of Mr. Trump’s deference to tech evangelists and investors like Mr. Sacks who are deeply skeptical of imposing additional guardrails or regulation.

And they worry about embracing any ideas for regulation, especially after Mr. Sacks and others persuaded the president at the last minute to pull back on an executive order earlier this year that would have required mandatory government reviews of new A.I. models. It was replaced with a voluntary review regime.

Mr. Trump seems driven chiefly by the sense that A.I. is the way to economic growth and nothing can be allowed to stand in its way.

He has long promised that his presidencies would bring on a manufacturing boom that would usher in a new “golden age” for America. His first-term promise was that he would achieve that by reviving heavy industries, claiming his policies would bring coal mining jobs back to the deindustrialized Midwest.

But those jobs did not materialize. When he returned to the presidency for his second term, Mr. Trump believed the tech companies’ gargantuan capital expenditures could be the necessary fuel to run the economy hot.

He had latched onto this idea during the late campaign season. In a private meeting with OpenAI executives in June 2024, Mr. Trump discussed with them the idea of creating a version of “Operation Warp Speed” — his all-of-government enterprise to fast-track Covid vaccines — for the building of data centers.

Ever since, he has been determined to fuel A.I. growth at nearly any political cost, to keep alive what he has referred to as “the golden goose.” Mr. Trump, a real estate developer, is eager to keep building, dismissing the concerns of states and towns that want to slow or halt construction.

“The robots will not be taking over,” Mr. Trump insisted when he called into a large conference where Mr. Sacks and Mr. Huang were onstage this week. “The A.I. will not be taking over the rest of the world.”

President Trump has called fears about out-of-control A.I. an “open hoax.” But behind the scenes, some of his aides have been grappling with a much more complicated question: whether the government needs to review new A.I. models and whether Washington should regulate the technology. That debate, largely hidden from public view, is considerably more robust than you might gather from listening to the president. And with Xi Jinping expected to visit next week, the question of whether the United States and China can reach a preliminary accord on A.I. is taking on added urgency.

Maggie Haberman contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump’s Compensation Fund Is Dead. Could He Find Other Ways to Pay Allies?
item.description:
Even though the Justice Department has repeatedly vowed that it has scrapped its plans to create a $1.8 billion fund to compensate people who believe they have been politically prosecuted, questions have lingered about whether President Trump might find another way to funnel taxpayer money to his allies.

Could Mr. Trump simply create a different fund that would do something similar? Or could he use other legal avenues to award financial damages to his supporters — including the hundreds of rioters charged in connection with the attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021?

Those same issues were raised at a court hearing on Friday by a federal judge who has already barred the fund from moving forward. She said she remained concerned that the Trump administration might use novel means to make payments to people who share its political viewpoint.

“I think the anti-weaponization fund — that entity — is gone,” the judge, Leonie M. Brinkema, said during the hearing. “But is there a functional equivalent of that going on now?”

The judge quickly added, “The issues underlying this case are alive and kicking.”

The case she was referring to is a lawsuit filed in Federal District Court in Alexandria, Va., that has challenged the legality of both the compensation fund and a separate measure granting Mr. Trump, his family and his businesses expansive protections from all past tax investigations.

The two provisions emerged from a backroom deal reached this spring between Justice Department officials and Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers to end a different lawsuit that the president had filed accusing the Internal Revenue Service of allowing some of his tax returns to be leaked to reporters.

That suit was denounced in July by a federal judge in Florida who described it as an improper exercise in self-dealing given that Mr. Trump had sought money from a government agency that he effectively controls. The Florida judge, Kathleen M. Williams, also accused the president and top officials at the Justice Department — including Attorney General Todd Blanche — of seeking to manipulate the court system to lend a veneer of validity to the secret negotiations that ended the suit and led to the creation of the fund and tax protections.

At the hearing in Virginia, the task that Judge Brinkema faced was to consider a request by the government to dismiss the suit that has challenged both those measures.

The Justice Department has argued that the claims against the fund are moot because Mr. Blanche has said several times that it is dead. The department has also asserted that the claims against the tax provision should be tossed out because the plaintiff that raised them — the union representing I.R.S. workers — lacks the legal standing to make the challenge.

Judge Brinkema, a Clinton appointee, seemed open to the Justice Department’s assertions, recognizing that the fund that the suit set out to destroy effectively no longer exists. She also appeared to buy into the government’s argument concerning standing, saying that no evidence existed that I.R.S. workers had actually been asked to stop an audit of Mr. Trump’s taxes.

Still, while the judge held off for now on ruling on the motion to dismiss the suit, she was unable to let go of the basic principles that motivated it in the first place.

She noted, for example, that after the compensation fund was set aside, several Jan. 6 rioters filed lawsuits against the government, claiming they were wrongly prosecuted and asking for financial damages. While the judge acknowledged that the Justice Department was, for the moment, “properly opposing” those suits, she raised the possibility that officials might at some point change their mind and quietly seek to settle them.

The Trump administration in fact has a history of settling lawsuits filed by its allies.

In March, it agreed to pay Michael T. Flynn, Mr. Trump’s former national security adviser, $1.25 million to settle claims that he was wrongfully prosecuted for making false statements to federal agents investigating ties between Russia and Mr. Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.

Around the same time, the administration offered a similar sum to settle a lawsuit brought by Carter Page, an adviser to the 2016 Trump campaign who was wiretapped during the Russia investigation.

Judge Brinkema had similar qualms about the measure granting tax protections to the president and his family. She noted that while Judge Williams’s ruling in Florida did not kill the provision outright, it effectively “castrated” it and could make it difficult to enforce in the future.

Moreover, she pointed to a statute that forbids the president from directly or indirectly ordering a tax audit from being opened or closed. And while she conceded that the statute usually allows the attorney general to start or end audits, she wondered whether the exception was valid if the attorney general had no independence from the president.

“You have the president able to control the very people who are supposed to be independent actors here,” Judge Brinkema said, adding that was “very problematic.”

item.title: Cost of Iran War Estimated at $43.6 Billion
item.description:
The cost of the war in Iran was $43.6 billion through Sept. 3, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60 percent of the expenses, the Pentagon told Congress this week.

The estimate for the first time offered an unclassified breakdown of costs incurred by each of the armed services, as well as for specific categories, like damaged or destroyed weaponry.

The Air Force, for instance, has spent $6.6 billion to pay for operating dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons. The Navy has incurred $2.2 billion in costs to deploy more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers. And it has cost the Army $1.6 billion to sustain its forces in the region. Overall, more than 50,000 troops are assigned to the war mission, according to U.S. Central Command.

Congressional officials shared the cost estimates with The New York Times after it was provided to congressional national security committees.

Since the war started on Feb. 28, the military has burned through $28.1 billion in munitions, seriously depleting global stockpiles of some critical weapons, like Patriot air-defense interceptors, and siphoning supplies from U.S. military commands in Asia and Europe.

The Pentagon has spent $4.3 billion to replace dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft and other weaponry and equipment. It has spent $633 million to move and support several thousand Special Operations commandos in the region.

The information also revealed spending in other critical battlefield accounts, with the military spending $23.5 million on “in-house medical support” for U.S. service members, according to one congressional official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the information provided to lawmakers. The Pentagon says 18 service members have been killed in the war and more than 830 injured.

U.S. Transportation Command spent $92.1 million to move supplies and equipment, and U.S. Cyber Command spent $10.5 million on “cybersupport operations,” the official said.

In a statement, the Defense Department said on Friday, “We do not comment on leaked documents and always keep Congress informed.”

The department’s figures are almost certainly on the low side, congressional officials said on Friday, noting that the Pentagon acknowledged that its estimate did not include $1.5 billion for fuel and other costs that the Trump administration has asked for in a supplemental request to pay for the war.

The costs to repair or replace U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks — such as the Navy’s base in Manama, Bahrain — also were not included in the information sent to Congress, as the Pentagon has indicated it may close or not rebuild them. If the military or host countries do rebuild, congressional officials say the bill could run tens of billions of dollars.

A report released this week by the Defense Department inspector general said the State Department estimated that its embassies, consulates and other diplomatic facilities in the Middle East had suffered about $184 million in damage from Iranian strikes.

The unclassified Pentagon cost estimates provided to Congress offer a rare glimpse into the financial accounting of the war, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his top aides have largely kept under wraps.

This week, the Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan scorekeeper, said the war in Iran cost the United States roughly $38 billion through Aug. 1 and significantly depleted U.S. munitions.

In a 19-page analysis, which the office said had been limited because the Defense Department did not respond to its requests for information, the C.B.O. projected that the war would continue to cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month, and that rebuilding depleted U.S. stockpiles could take “at least five years.”

The budget office said it relied on government databases and public reports to make its assessment because the Pentagon declined to provide any information.

The office’s estimate was roughly in line with congressional testimony delivered in late July by Mr. Hegseth, who estimated then that the war had cost $37.5 billion.

Mr. Hegseth and the Trump administration are requesting as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and pay for new weapons and personnel.

item.title: St. Paul Mayor’s Behavior Faulted After Police Chief’s Complaint
item.description:
Mayor Kaohly Her of St. Paul, Minn., treated colleagues in an “offensive and inappropriate” manner and created an “uncomfortable work environment,” the city’s top human resources official said Friday.

An independent review into the mayor’s workplace conduct was carried out after the police chief, Axel Henry, filed a complaint in March accusing Ms. Her of sexually harassing him and other employees during her first months on the job.

In a two-page summary of the case, Kamaria Kassim, St. Paul’s director of human resources, said investigators did not substantiate that claim. City officials did not release the report itself and would not say whether they intended to make it public.

Ms. Her, who was sworn in early this year, said that she was relieved that the review by a law firm did not find that she sexually harassed subordinates.

“At times, I became too informal in my communications and crossed lines that are not consistent with the standards set forth in the city’s workplace conduct policy,” Ms. Her said in a statement on Friday. “I apologize for any discomfort I caused.”

The mayor said that she had “always worked to be approachable as a leader and build strong working relationships.” She added: “I attempt to connect with people to build camaraderie.”

Ms. Her did not respond to a request for an interview.

In her role as mayor, Ms. Her must work closely with the police chief as St Paul, the state’s capital and second-largest city, as it wrestles with a budget shortfall and a contentious debate over homeless encampments.

The formal complaint from Chief Henry, a police force veteran whom Ms. Her’s predecessor appointed in 2022 to a six-year term, alleged several actions that he said amounted to unlawful sexual harassment and created a toxic work environment.

He said they included sending a text message to an officer that included a sexual reference involving a hot dog, comments about the breasts of a female police officer and making moaning sounds while working out at the police department gym.

Chris Madel, a lawyer representing Chief Axel, in a statement called the summary “a sanitized, self-serving whitewash of an investigation.” He added: “No amount of bureaucratic wordsmithing by the city’s H.R. department can make witnesses — or what they heard — disappear.”

When he filed the complaint, Chief Henry notified the city he was considering filing a lawsuit.

Ms. Kassim’s letter said the investigation had found no evidence that the mayor made sexual noises while exercising, or had retaliated against or sexually harassed city employees.

It recommended that Ms. Her hire an executive coach at her own expense, attend training on workplace conduct and “maintain appropriate professional boundaries.” The mayor said she would follow those suggestions.

A human resources official will monitor whether Mayor Her is complying with workplace rules for the next six months, Ms. Kassim wrote. The letter does not say whether the mayor would face discipline.

Ms. Her became the first female and Asian American mayor of the city of about 307,000 residents last year after she defeated Melvin Carter, a two-term incumbent who was once her boss. Ms. Her pledged to be a better fiscal steward, to make City Hall more responsive to residents and to “ensure our city runs efficiently and transparently.”

Before becoming mayor, Ms. Her represented a St. Paul district in the Minnesota House of Representatives and served as policy director early in Mr. Carter’s administration.

Matt Wagenius, the mayor’s spokesman, did not respond to several questions on Friday, including whether the city planned to release the report and how much money the investigation had cost taxpayers.

Ms. Kassim, who was appointed by Mayor Her to her role in February, did not immediately respond to a request for an interview.

item.title: F.A.A. Has an Unusual Safety Request for the Top of Trump’s Arch: Fire
item.description:
President Trump’s planned 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington must have a constant flame atop the structure to make it safe for planes to pass by in one of the busiest airspaces in the country, the Federal Aviation Administration said.

In a hazard study released on Friday, the F.A.A. deemed the proposed arch, which would sit along a flight path less than a mile from Ronald Reagan National Airport, safe for air travel provided that Mr. Trump complies with recommended safety measures.

“The proposed structure should be appropriately marked/lighted with a nonstandard eternal flame and continuously floodlighted by searchlight projectors installed at three or more equidistant points around the base of the structure,” the study said.

In June, F.A.A. evaluators recommended that red, blinking obstruction lights similar to the ones atop the Washington Monument be added to the arch — a common measure for large structures that go up near airports. But upon further review, the agency altered the safety provisions.

A White House spokesman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The mammoth arch would sit directly in the paths of flights in and out of Reagan National Airport.

Mr. Trump has said the arch, which he has proposed building between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, must be taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. He has said the arch is meant to celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, though he has also said the arch is for himself.

The F.A.A. safety study was a step forward for Mr. Trump’s plans, which have not received final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission. The commission has authority over building projects on federally owned land in Washington. Last month, Mr. Trump named Mark Paoletta, a lawyer in his administration and a close associate of Justice Clarence Thomas’s, to lead the planning commission reviewing the arch.

A group of Vietnam War veterans has sued to stop construction, citing the lack of congressional approval for the project and arguing that the arch would obstruct the view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. A federal judge has for now ordered the administration not to begin major construction without first notifying her.

Among the criticisms of Mr. Trump’s planned arch is that it would disrupt the view of another eternal flame: the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, a presidential memorial at the gravesite of the former president in Arlington National Cemetery.

item.title: F.A.A. to Roll Out New A.I. Tool for Washington Airports
item.description:
The Trump administration plans to roll out a new A.I. air traffic control tool designed to predict and prevent flight delays in the Washington region starting Monday, as the opening step of an eventual nationwide deployment.

The tool, called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories, or SMART, is designed to analyze airline schedules, weather patterns and other potential air traffic interruptions to “predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur” and recommend alternate flight routes to avoid compound delays.

While the $875 million system is expected to be deployed nationwide by 2028, Monday’s rollout will be limited to the Washington region, affecting three airports: Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport.

Washington’s congested airspace, one of the busiest in the nation, has drawn particular scrutiny following the January 2025 midair collision between a commercial jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter that killed 67. The National Transportation Safety Board placed the blame for certain failures leading up to the crash on the Federal Aviation Administration.

The phased rollout is a chance for the administration to assess how well the new technology helps airlines and air traffic controllers avoid flight delays, and whether artificial intelligence can help those responsible for managing airline traffic circumvent potential interruptions more efficiently than they can on their own. The rollout comes amid a national uproar over the rapid development of A.I. models and bipartisan calls to rein in the industry, which President Trump and several of his deputies have flatly rejected.

Against that background, Transportation Department officials stress that the SMART system will not replace human operators or direct any changes to flight routes, but merely offer recommendations that controllers can choose to heed or ignore. The system will be located at the F.A.A.’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Warrenton, Va., which manages airspace traffic; officials will disseminate the A.I. recommendations to controllers at the regional towers and other air traffic facilities.

Transportation officials also pointed out that SMART is designed to analyze scheduling and congestion data over a month in advance to help predict when airports and airlines might be vulnerable to delays. But the rollout will begin modestly at first, with the A.I. system offering alternatives to avoid only same-day delays, such as those caused by weather, before being scaled up to its full potential.

“We’re excited to launch SMART and take another major step toward improving air travel for the American people,” the F.A.A. spokeswoman Hannah Walden said in a statement, calling SMART “a new tool that will fundamentally change the way we manage our skies.”

Yet the progress to this point has not been wholly smooth.

Federal transportation officials announced in June that they had awarded the contract to develop SMART to Air Space Intelligence, a Boston-based software company. At a congressional hearing this week, Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, asked Congress for billions more dollars to fully modernize air traffic control systems, arguing that new technologies are needed to “supercharge our ability to safely grow traffic and reduce the workload and strain on our controllers.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and other administration officials have criticized current air traffic control systems as outdated and touted new programs, including the new A.I. tool, as “a huge, massive build and upgrade.”

For a rollout to begin only a few months after the contract was awarded is uncommonly fast, according to officials and experts, some of whom stressed that the F.A.A. had to engage in extensive conversations to allay concerns among airlines and controllers that the A.I. system might prove more problematic than helpful.

Robert Mann, a former airline executive who is now an aviation industry consultant, said that SMART may suggest better flight plans, but it is unlikely to address the major problems associated with delays, which happen after a flight plan is filed.

“Whether it’s on the ground or in flight or in the terminal area,” Mr. Mann said, “you’re up against a whole bunch of other traffic which arrives roughly the same time, and that’s because they’ve experienced the same sort of random delays on the ground, en route, and in the arrivals area that you are.”

While airlines might cooperate with the program initially, he added that they might come to view it as an intrusion from the F.A.A., because they carefully plan and manage their flight schedules well in advance and changes are costly.

“We’ll see how long that acquiescence lasts,” Mr. Mann added.

The rollout also comes as the F.A.A. has struggled to solve a chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. While the agency has insisted that the new A.I. system will not displace or replace human employees, the Trump administration and the union representing air traffic controllers are currently locked in a dispute about how many controllers the F.A.A. needs to hire to make up staffing shortfalls.

A year ago, the F.A.A. published a report suggesting that it would need 14,633 controllers to be fully staffed; this spring, it revised that estimate down by more than 2,000 positions, stressing that more efficient scheduling could offset the need for more hires. As of this April, the F.A.A. reported having more than 11,000 fully certified controllers.

A spokesman for the National Air Traffic Controllers Association said in a statement that the union “believes any new technology should complement and not replace the experience, training and professional judgment of air traffic controllers who are responsible for the safety of the National Airspace System.” It added that the group had not been part of the design or testing process of the system.

item.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
item.description:
The Russian government has been targeting Americans with covert online disinformation operations seeking to undermine public confidence in November’s midterm elections, using a familiar playbook in an attempt to inject chaos into the voting season, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter.

Classified U.S. intelligence assessments from recent months have determined that the Kremlin has again authorized a digital influence campaign to peddle content across social media in hopes of seeding or amplifying domestic divisions around the election season, the officials said.

The assessments did not find evidence of attempts to take aim at voting machinery in a way that could compromise the actual voting process, the officials added. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss classified information, did not specify the efforts to influence attitudes online. But experts in Russian disinformation have spotted some social media campaigns in recent weeks that use artificial intelligence to create fake videos of Hollywood celebrities talking about key battleground Senate races.

The disinformation campaign appeared to be less extensive or coordinated than at least some of Russia’s prior efforts in American elections, some of the officials said. Since 2016, the Kremlin has initiated online influence operations in every American federal election cycle, according to previously declassified assessments. The officials added that U.S. spy agencies see Moscow as less interested in midterm races than in presidential contests and as distracted by its grinding war with Ukraine.

Still, the push to inflame the electorate comes as President Trump has repeatedly sought to challenge the integrity of American democracy. In July, Mr. Trump gave a televised prime-time address on election security in which he claimed there were severe vulnerabilities in U.S. voting systems and accused American officials of a yearslong “cover-up” to conceal efforts by China and others to influence elections.

He has instructed a task force to declassify documents purporting to support his narratives of rampant voter fraud and foreign tampering, but those files, which were heavily redacted, did not reveal major new weaknesses in the country’s election systems or show that foreign governments had manipulated any votes.

Some of the officials said the main goal of the Russian influence operations appeared to be to sow chaos rather than aid one particular party, though the examples that independent disinformation researchers in recent weeks have attributed to Russia have exclusively attacked Democratic candidates in swing states.

The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Russian Embassy did not respond to requests for comment. Russia has historically denied U.S. allegations of election meddling.

Some intelligence assessments have also found that Iran, too, may engage in influence operations around the November election as well, the officials said, though little activity had been documented in classified channels that traced to Tehran. The country, which has been locked in a war with the United States since February, sought to spread propaganda undermining Mr. Trump in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, and officials said it was reasonable to expect the regime to do so again.

Last month, Meta released a report highlighting a small network of accounts on Facebook and Instagram originating in Iran that focused on U.S. politics. The network’s content, some of which was generated with artificial intelligence, included “anti-Republican views,” Meta said.

The U.S. intelligence findings also said China could be willing to engage in influence operations by targeting individual congressional races or members of Congress whom Beijing sees as adversarial to its interests, officials said.

That approach, too, would echo its activity in past election seasons, but the U.S. intelligence assessments found that Beijing may ultimately steer clear for fear of blowback, the officials said. In general, China is more careful in order to avoid being caught, while Russia and Iran are seen as less bothered about being discovered, current and former U.S. officials said.

In 2016, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia ordered a multipronged interference effort that sought to denigrate Hillary Clinton, the Democratic nominee, and bolster the electoral prospects of her Republican rival, Mr. Trump, U.S. spy agencies concluded. Multiple audits of those intelligence findings, including a multiyear investigation by the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee, corroborated those conclusions.

Researchers in Europe and the United States who track Russian disinformation campaigns have seen recent signs of Russian activity. In two separate waves over the past week, a network previously linked to Kremlin trolls posted a series of videos on X and BlueSky that appeared to rely on A.I. to churn out baseless claims against Democrats running for Senate in closely contested races. Elements of the campaign were reported earlier by MS NOW.

The posts attacked the candidates using themes that Mr. Trump and the Republican Party have relied on to disparage Democrats, including accusations of corruption, antisemitism and support for gay and transgender rights.

The posts included false or unsubstantiated claims in videos devised to seem as if they came from prominent news organizations, including CNN, the BBC and The New York Times.

Among those targeted were Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces re-election in Georgia, and other challengers who have a chance of giving Democrats a majority in the Senate: Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Troy Jackson in Maine, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, Mary Peltola in Alaska, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas, and Joshua Turek in Iowa.

Graphika, a threat analysis company, attributed the blitz to a Kremlin-linked operation that experts have called Operation Overload or Matryoshka, which often impersonates real news organizations to spread fabricated content.

A post that appeared on Thursday mimicked a Times video featuring an image of the actress Jamie Lee Curtis with subtitles criticizing the Democrats for their policies on transgender issues. “There’s not even a scintilla of truth in that,” the actress’ publicist, Heidi Schaeffer, said in an interview.

By the end of the day, the post had been viewed nearly 200,000 times, according to X’s count. X, which did not respond to a request for comment, removed some of the posts that appeared earlier in the week, but many remain online.

The posts employed Russian tactics familiar from previous elections in the United States and Europe.

Jean Le Roux, a senior researcher at Graphika, noted that the American content appeared shortly after elections in Germany and Sweden concluded.

“We’re definitely expecting it to ramp up,” he said of the Russian effort. “I don’t think they’re going to stop. I think that we’re seeing the initial kickoff of the U.S. election focused campaigning.”

item.title: Sympathy for a Dog in San Diego Who Seemed to Greet an Intruder
item.description:
So much for guarding the castle.

When an intruder broke into Dante Rowley’s home in San Diego this month, home-security cameras captured his golden retriever, Nash, hiding and panting under the dining room table. The dog stayed there as the man helped himself to yogurt and lay down on a blanket.

Then Nash made his move: he approached the man as he walked near the door, and looked up at him, with his tail wagging and a plush toy in his mouth.

Why didn’t he bark? Was he eager to play?

Where many viewers of the video saw a dog trying to have fun when he should be growling, animal behavior experts offered their own interpretations. Some embraced the idea that Nash was eager to make friends, and others said the dog’s behavior was a sign of an anxious animal.

Dr. Katherine A. Houpt, a professor emeritus at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, thinks Nash is a rather affable retriever.

“The dog wanted someone to play with, and the burglar is as good as anyone,” she said. “It’s a breed that’s often friendly and, apparently, the owners made sure he was socialized with people. So he doesn’t think something awful is going to come in the door, but something fun, a playmate.”

Dr. Carlo Siracusa, a professor of clinical small animal behavior and welfare at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine, had a different view. Hiding, panting and holding a chew toy can all be signs that a dog is stressed, he said. Even a wagging tail can be a sign of increased alertness and emotional arousal. Nash, he said, might simply have approached the man because he was near the door, and the dog wanted to get out.

Dr. Siracusa pointed out that Nash also approached the police with a chew toy in his mouth and scurried outside when they came through the door, holding guns.

“It’s very difficult to understand exactly what the dog had in mind, but I don’t see any evidence the dog is trying to be friendly with the intruder or the police,” Dr. Siracusa said. “This is a human interpretation. It’s not an objective reading of the body language.”

In general, he said, a dog’s response to an intruder comes down to “individual variability,” and, to a lesser extent, their breed. Some may feel sharp fear and respond aggressively, he said, just as some humans might startle more than others when they hear an unfamiliar noise in the night.

Mr. Rowley and his fiancée, Stephanie Calderon, had been preparing to fly home from Chicago on Sept. 5 when his security camera sent him an alert. Someone was breaking into his house. The cameras recorded the man using a ladder to climb through a second-story window and then wander around, with his shirt and shoes off.

Mr. Rowley called the San Diego police, who arrived within minutes, sent a drone inside the house and then arrested the man. He was charged with burglary, vandalism, battery on an officer and drug possession, the police said.

Mr. Rowley said that Nash was unharmed, as was his other dog, Ollie, a longhaired dachshund that had run into the backyard. (Mr. Rowley’s brother, who lives down the street, had been dog sitting.)

“Honestly, Nash is just friendly; he’s not a guard dog by any means, so when I saw his reaction, I was surprised that he wasn’t more excited,” Mr. Rowley said on Friday. “Usually, when he sees new people, he runs over and jumps all over them and is just on them 24-7.”

Marc Bekoff, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and the author of “Dogs Demystified: An A-Z Guide to All Things Canine,” said that a dog’s breed doesn’t determine whether it’s going to be a good guard dog.

“You could train a beagle to be a guard dog,” he said. “To me, it just comes down — like with humans — to early rearing.”

Dr. Bekoff said he wasn’t surprised that Nash greeted the intruder with a toy in his mouth. He said he has a part-Doberman mutt who would have done the same thing.

“I see a total love-muffin,” he said. “What I see is a healthy, socialized dog. He just want to play.”

Dr. Houpt agreed.

“It’s a friendly dog, and the dog doesn’t do a background check before he interacts with people,” she said. “So we need more Nashes, is what I’m trying to say.”

item.title: Trump Has Tried to Ban Reporters From Government Spaces Before
item.description:
The Trump administration has repeatedly moved to ban reporters from the White House and other government property.

In January 2025, Mr. Trump tried to bar Associated Press journalists from parts of the White House, including the Oval Office and Air Force One. The A.P. has sued to restore its access, but that case remains in litigation; in the meantime, A.P. photographers have had continued access to the Oval Office. Its print journalists have had more limited access.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has also placed limits on reporters’ access to the Pentagon, including a requirement that all journalists be accompanied by an official escort while in the building. The Pentagon also closed the work space used for years by journalists with credentials to cover the military. The New York Times sued over the restrictions, and the litigation continues.

During his first term, Mr. Trump revoked a White House pass for Jim Acosta, the former CNN journalist. CNN succeeded in restoring Mr. Acosta’s press credentials in court.

Mr. Trump also tried to temporarily suspend the press pass of a reporter who traded caustic comments with Sebastian Gorka, a right-wing commentator who worked briefly in the White House. The reporter successfully sued to restore his credential.

item.title: U.S. Has Reached Security Deal on Greenland, Trump Says
item.description:
President Trump said on Friday that his administration had reached a deal with Denmark and Greenland to expand the U.S. security presence in Greenland, a semiautonomous Danish territory, raising the possibility of a diplomatic solution to a U.S.-made threat that nearly upended the Western alliance.

The full contours of the deal Mr. Trump was describing were not immediately clear, but shortly after his announcement, leaders of Greenland and Denmark issued statements indicating they expected an agreement to be signed next week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The two sides described the agreement in very different terms. Mr. Trump claimed the United States had secured “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland, while the Danish prime minister said the deal “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of the Kingdom of Denmark.

That description would mean the agreement fell well short of Mr. Trump’s longstanding demand of total control over Greenland.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump said that “anything less” than U.S. ownership of Greenland would be “unacceptable.” He said possession of the territory was “psychologically important” to him.

Instead, what Mr. Trump described on Friday was a deal that would prevent U.S. adversaries from having a base on Greenland and expand the U.S. military presence in the territory. In his social media post, Mr. Trump said that under the deal, “no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”

Officials from Denmark and Greenland did not immediately confirm that the United States had received such veto power — a U.S. demand that they had strongly opposed in closed-door negotiations in recent months. And two people close to the negotiations said Mr. Trump’s declaration of permanent control over Greenland’s security exaggerated the degree of new powers the United States would get over the territory. The U.S. military will be working with its counterparts in Denmark and Greenland under the agreement rather than asserting control over them, a U.S. military official said.

Still, the apparent deal, reached after months of high-stakes confidential talks with officials from the United States, Greenland and Denmark, could mark an off-ramp to an issue that caused widespread concern among NATO allies earlier this year.

Mr. Trump said in his post that the United States “will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many.”

He also said the United States would “FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland,” even though the existing U.S. agreement with Denmark to host American military bases on Greenland does not have a time limit.

The United States first established a military presence in Greenland during World War II, and in 1951 reached an agreement with Denmark granting it broad freedom to operate military installations on the island.

The 1951 pact allowed for access by the forces of NATO nations. But it did not explicitly restrict the presence of “adversary” nations, as Mr. Trump claimed on Friday the new agreement would do. Under the new deal, countries that are not part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization would not be permitted to build a base or maintain a military presence in Greenland, according to a State Department official detailing the deal under the condition of anonymity.

Given that Greenland is alliance territory, the prospect of a non-NATO nation building bases there was already highly unlikely.

The agreement would also remain in effect even if Greenland were to become an independent nation, the official said.

“This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

Denmark still manages defense issues for Greenland, and one of the Trump administration’s goals has been to ensure that even if Greenland achieves independence, which many Greenlanders support, that would not change the access the U.S. military has today.

Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said in a statement on Friday night that the agreement would strengthen “our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and is therefore also good for NATO and Europe.”

Ms. Frederiksen also said the deal “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, said in a statement that the agreement “recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all.”

Mr. Trump has been pushing to acquire Greenland since his first term, but leaders in both Denmark and Greenland have rejected the idea. As tensions with Mr. Trump peaked in January, the Danish military developed detailed plans to blow up airfields in Greenland in the event of an American invasion. Danish soldiers were even sent to Greenland equipped with explosives and blood supplies, though the worst-case scenarios never materialized.

The action then turned to confidential talks between the United States, Greenland and Denmark. Negotiators met in Washington about once a month. In those talks, the United States discussed cooperation with Greenland on natural resources and expanding the U.S. military presence on the territory. According to officials close to the talks, American negotiators had been insisting on veto power over any major investment deals in Greenland to box out competitors like Russia and China.

During the Cold War, the U.S. military maintained more than a dozen installations on the island but all were eventually shut down except one, the Pituffik Space Base, on the northwest coast. In recent weeks, American military officers have been visiting the island with plans to reopen several old bases. Just this week, Denmark’s public broadcaster reported that a group of American soldiers were surveying the runway in Narsarsuaq, in southern Greenland.

Imran Bayoumi, a deputy director for the GeoStrategy Initiative at the Atlantic Council, said the agreement announced on Friday offered “little in the way of new content.”

“It’s likely that Washington could have achieved many of these outcomes through negotiations with Denmark and Greenland directly, without worsening the relationship,” Mr. Bayoumi said. “Nonetheless, it gives the U.S. a critical footprint in the Arctic at a time when the region is becoming more important.”

Eric Schmitt and Michael Crowley contributed reporting from Washington, and Maya Tekeli from Copenhagen.

item.title: Republicans Are Now the ‘Elitist’ Party, Voters Say
item.description:
In American politics, “elite” is a four-letter word.

For years, Democrats have been derided as the “liberal elite.” That caricature began to look more like reality as the party lost working-class voters and gained wealthier and better educated ones. And strategists struggled to turn the insult back on President Trump, who has maintained a cultural connection to the working class despite his status as a wealthy owner of golf courses and gilded clubs.

The dynamic might be shifting.

Deep in the data from The Times’s and Siena University’s national poll this week is a figure that I found quite striking: Voters are now more likely to see Republicans than Democrats as “elitist.”

Tonight, we’re going to zoom in on that finding, which comes as shifting voter perceptions — and unease about the economy — force Republicans to confront the possibility of broader problems with the coalition that carried Trump to victory.

When our pollsters asked likely voters which party they think the word “elitist” describes, 43 percent of them said Republicans and 33 percent said Democrats.

The Times’s polling editor, Ruth Igielnik, told me that we asked the same question in 2022. Back then, Republicans and Democrats were about tied — 35 percent for Democrats, 36 percent for Republicans — so the new figures, Ruth said, represent a notable shift.

The bump was driven in part by independent voters. In 2022, 36 percent of independents described Republicans as the more elitist party. This year, that figure was 45 percent.

In the latest poll, men were about evenly split on the party they viewed as most elitist, but women chose Republicans by a 20-point margin.

Every age group was more likely to identify Republicans as “elitist,” although it was 18- to 29-year-olds who did so most decisively: 59 percent to 27 percent.

Yesterday, my colleague Sophia June and I called up some of these voters. We wanted to talk with independents — and we were especially interested to speak with those who had supported Trump in 2024 but now viewed Republicans as the more elitist party.

Interestingly, none of the voters we spoke with brought up the projects Democrats have seized on to paint Trump as out of touch, like his White House ballroom or his penchant for gilding the Oval Office. They described something broader: a Republican Party that, they felt, had stopped looking out for everybody.

“That’s what Trump’s doing to America now: The people that are ‘in with him,’ who look or act a certain way, are the ones that are gonna be given an opportunity,” Lauren Wilson, 40, of Cranford, N.J., said. Wilson, a stay-at-home parent who backed Trump in 2024, said she’s planning to vote for Democrats in November.

Rebecca Schneider-Kaplan, an educator who lives in Staten Island, said she voted for Trump in the last election but soured on him because he viewed himself as “untouchable,” insulated from consequences the rest of us might face if we posted impulsively on social media or, you know, suddenly tried to rename a lake.

“He thinks he’s above everything,” Schneider-Kaplan said.

Jesus Estrada, 21, who lives in Pasadena, Texas, and works in a fabrication plant, brought up Trump’s taxes. “Donald Trump basically had to pay almost nothing,” said Estrada, who did not vote in 2024. He added, “Elitist is the word I use for the 1 percent because they’re doing loopholes for taxes.”

And Jerry Jacob, 37, told me that, these days, Republicans seem to be “in their own world.” He recalled their vaunted tax cut bill, which showered benefits on the highest earners, as evidence of a fundamental disconnect.

“When they’re asked questions about how the American public is doing, they give these answers like, ‘Everything is fine,’ when people are struggling,” Jacob said.

Jacob said he voted for Trump in 2024, Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2016. I told him I might have to call him back in 2028.

Catch Me Up

Trump said this afternoon that he plans to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House for reporting “fake news.”

A watchdog group says Trump’s oversight of a $400 million super PAC — which he calls “my money that I control” — violates federal law. But the complaint is unlikely to change anything: The F.E.C., which regulates campaign finance, doesn’t even have enough confirmed members to meet.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is spending $300,000 to help boost Democrats in New York, Shane Goldmacher reported today. I found it especially interesting that the money is intended for organizing rather than advertising.

quote of the day

That was President Trump. He has publicly downplayed fears of an A.I. doomsday as a “hoax.” The Times reported today that his bullishness on A.I. is rooted in his concern that an A.I. slowdown could harm the economy. Some of his aides, though, are worried about the dangers of rogue A.I. agents.

Some Republican candidates are subtly backing away from the Trump administration. The Times’s Bayliss Wagner sent us this update from Iowa.

When Vice President JD Vance rallied for Republicans in Council Bluffs, Iowa, today, one very important Iowa Republican was absent: Ashley Hinson, the party’s nominee in a closer-than-expected Senate race.

Hinson said last September that she wanted to be “Trump’s top ally in the United States Senate.” But she has since distanced herself from his administration as Iowans fume over high fuel, grocery and fertilizer prices. (Last month, she went on Fox News to implore Trump not to cut tariffs on foreign ground beef, saying it would hurt struggling cattle ranchers.)

The pivot reflects the difficult headwinds that Hinson, a congresswoman and former TV news anchor, faces as she tries to keep the seat red. Read my profile here.

Related: Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a television ad yesterday criticizing Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Hitting the Road

Want to know where the parties’ attention is focused in these final weeks before Election Day? Look where some of their biggest names are traveling in the coming days:

Kamala Harris is scheduled to appear in Michigan early next week to campaign with Abdul El-Sayed, Democrats’ progressive Senate nominee. El-Sayed needs support from moderates if he hopes to win in purple Michigan.

Pete Buttigieg is traveling to San Antonio for a rally with Katy Padilla Stout, the Democratic House candidate in Texas’ 23rd District. Trump won the district by 15 points in 2024. But the Republican candidate there, Brandon Herrera, has come under fire for past Nazi jokes and vulgar comments about women.

Photo of the Week

The fate of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington got even murkier this week, as the center’s Trump-allied board abruptly shuttered the building after a judge said the president could not put his name on its facade.

The photo above, captured on Wednesday by The Times’s Kenny Holston, suggested one possible outcome: Through the windows of Air Force One, Trump, in his trademark red hat, can be seen reviewing a poster board with the words: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

Does that mean Trump plans to tear down the Kennedy Center? The White House has refused to answer questions about it.

ONE LAST THING

On Sept. 18, 1851 — 175 years ago today — The New York Times published its first issue. That edition, which was put together by candlelight, was four pages long and cost a penny.

Times journalists are revisiting remarkable moments from the paper’s early days. Read the story of Samuel Wilkeson Jr., our reporter at the Battle of Gettysburg, who happened upon the body of his own son on the battlefield and wrote, “My pen is heavy.”

For more: Can you guess what classic band our critic called “hoarsely incoherent?” Or which iconic headline editors of the past felt warranted an exclamation point? Take our quiz on Times history.

Sophia June and Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Appeals Court Restricts Trump Administration Deportation Effort
item.description:
The Trump administration will face new requirements before it is allowed to deport people to countries other than their nation of origin, an appeals court ruled on Friday.

The ruling, by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, requires that immigrants facing deportation to so-called third countries be given more due process beforehand — “a meaningful opportunity” to raise fears of persecution or torture. In a 55-page opinion with no dissent, a three-judge panel from the court rejected arguments from the Trump administration that it receives “assurances” from foreign governments that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured and that such communications should be sufficient.

The administration’s current policy “conflicts” with laws and regulations that protect detainees from torture, the judges ruled, and added that they were rejecting an attempt by the Homeland Security Department to carve out an exception to those rules “from whole cloth.”

If the ruling remains in place, it will impose a substantial and time-consuming hurdle on Mr. Trump’s third-country deportation program. The practice of sending deportees to faraway and sometimes dangerous countries, often with just a few hours’ notice, has been one of the administration’s highest-profile attempts to create uncertainty for immigrants already in the United States.

The administration has sent migrants to nations including South Sudan, Liberia and Equatorial Guinea as part of the program. In interviews with The New York Times, some migrants deported to third countries have made harrowing allegations that they were abused by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The Homeland Security Department has said detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” while in ICE custody, and denied that anyone has been beaten or tortured.

In March, the appeals panel temporarily blocked a ruling by Judge Brian E. Murphy of Massachusetts imposing the new requirements. Friday’s order lifts that block, putting most of the new legal hurdles to third-country deportations into place.

The administration can now appeal the ruling to a larger First Circuit panel or to the Supreme Court.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The case already reached the Supreme Court last year, when the justices agreed to allow eight men who had been sent to Djibouti in violation of a preliminary order from Judge Murphy to be sent onward to South Sudan. That ruling dealt with the issue on a temporary basis, while litigation over it moved forward.

The appeals court on Friday struck down one of the requirements that Judge Murphy had attempted to impose on D.H.S. Judge Murphy would have required the department to prioritize deportees’ home countries as destinations, but the appeals court said that could not be legally mandated.

In a statement, Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the migrants who brought the lawsuit, called Friday’s ruling “a major victory for the basic principle that the government cannot deport people to an unknown country without first telling them where they are being sent and giving them a meaningful opportunity to explain why they would face persecution or torture there.”

The unanimous opinion was written by Judge Seth R. Aframe, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Also on the panel were Judge Jeffrey R. Howard, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, and Judge Lara E. Montecalvo, another appointee of Mr. Biden. Judge Murphy is also a Biden appointee.

item.title: Kennedy Center Supporters Rally Amid Speculation About Possible Demolition
item.description:
A large group of demonstrators locked arms to form a human chain around the Kennedy Center on Friday evening to protest President Trump’s efforts to close and remake the center in his image, amid speculation about a possible effort to demolish the building.

Hundreds of demonstrators, many of them performing artists and workers at the Kennedy Center, sang and played music as they circled the building and the sun set over the embattled cultural institution.

Late Wednesday night, photojournalists captured a series of images through the windows of Air Force One that showed Mr. Trump reviewing a large poster board with what looked like a rendering of a construction site beneath the title: “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

The photos, which circulated online ahead of the rally, appeared to spur turnout. Several demonstrators said they had seen the images but dismissed the possibility of a demolition as another one of Mr. Trump’s publicity stunts. Organizers celebrated a previous court victory removing Mr. Trump’s name from the center and said they hoped that the center would soon reopen, after the board, led by Mr. Trump, moved to close it earlier this week.

“It seems pretty performative,” said David Novy, 51, who attended the rally and has been coming to performances at the Kennedy Center since he was in high school in the 1990s, and is a subscriber to the center’s ballet performances, the Washington National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra. Those groups have scattered their performances to other venues in the Washington area during the Kennedy Center’s temporary shutdown.

The images of the apparent demolition plan have been incorporated into a previously filed lawsuit over the fate of the Kennedy Center, which after a disastrous year and a half under Mr. Trump’s stewardship, has had plummeting ticket sales and a talent exodus. The center was closed temporarily this week over significant safety concerns, center officials said, after a large chunk of plaster fell from the ceiling.

The crowd, pressed up against security barriers surrounding the center, enveloped the concrete pavilion in front of it, spilled out across 25th Street and onto an adjacent grass lawn. One woman was forcibly escorted away from the building by security guards wearing hard hats after defying the safety perimeter.

Many of the artists at the protest had previously performed at the Kennedy Center, including the Gay Men’s Chorus of Washington, D.C., which had a planned concert canceled last year amid Mr. Trump’s efforts to reshape the institution’s programming. Other performers, like the Rapid Response Choir, have been fixtures of Washington-area protests since Mr. Trump returned to office last year.

Lynda Carter, the actress who played Wonder Woman, and local officials, including Robert White, an at-large member of the District of Columbia Council, attended and spoke at the rally.

“There is no way, no how,” Mr. White said, “that while I am standing, and while you people are standing, that he is going to take this building or take this city. So I plan that I will keep fighting, I will keep screaming, and I will throw some punches if need be.” The crowd cheered.

In an interview, Mr. White said he thought that Mr. Trump was lashing out after a federal judge ordered his administration to remove his name from the center — which was named by Congress to honor President John F. Kennedy after his assassination.

“Anything that he can’t have and try to steal, he wants to destroy,” Mr. White said. “But it is important that we not let him do that.”

Organizers had previously held demonstrations against Mr. Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center, but the turnout on Friday night was the largest in support of the performing arts institution. Tara Hoot, a drag queen performer and organizer of the demonstrations in support of the Kennedy Center, noted that a typical protest would draw between 60 and 100 people.

item.title: Air Force Officer Charged After Protesting Trump Says He Spoke to Defend Constitution
item.description:
An active-duty Air Force officer who was arrested in uniform at the Capitol in July after calling for President Trump’s impeachment made his first comments in court on Friday, in a case that could become a rare test of service members’ right to free speech.

Military prosecutors said during the preliminary hearing that Major Jason Watson betrayed regulations and the Constitution with “vitriolic attacks on the character of the president.” Their arguments came during what is known as an Article 32 hearing, an early step in the military justice process that helps determine whether a case should proceed to a court-martial.

Maj. Watson gave an unsworn statement in his defense, an uncommon move in such hearings. He told the investigating officer overseeing the proceedings, Major Joshua Wendell, that he was driven by his sworn duty to defend the Constitution, not partisanship.

“I spoke to change something I believed was wrong, in the open, under the weight of my own name and my own oath,” Maj. Watson said.

Several of the charges stem from his July arrest at a protest at the Capitol, during which he accused the president of violating the Constitution several times over. He pointed to Mr. Trump’s military actions in Iran and Venezuela, his sweeping immigration crackdown and his dismantling of many parts of the federal government.

Maj. Watson later gave a broadcast interview to CNN in August in which he repeated many of those criticisms, telling the anchor Erin Burnett that the president had failed the country and that he hoped his protest inspired other Americans to act.

Prosecutors also alleged that Maj. Watson was responsible for an anonymous Substack post from June 2025 that called Mr. Trump “a greedy, unintelligent, narcissistic, pathological liar, traitor, and coward.”

In an interview conducted before Maj. Watson was charged, his lawyer, Christopher Mutimer, said the airman was detained on his base the day after the CNN interview, after he reported for duty and informed his chain of command that he would not wear his uniform again. He has remained in pretrial confinement since.

Maj. Watson is charged with 10 violations of the military justice code under Article 88, for using “contemptuous” words against the president or other senior officials; Article 92, for failing to obey orders or regulations; and Article 133, for conduct unbecoming of an officer. He could potentially face years in prison, forfeiture of pay and benefits, and dishonorable discharge.

A member of the public was removed from the courtroom after making a brief interjection during the hearing, which lasted roughly four hours on Friday.

Maj. Wendell, who presided over the proceeding, is expected to recommend later this month whether Maj. Watson’s case should proceed to court-martial. If so, he will also recommend whether it should be a special court-martial, the equivalent of civilian misdemeanor court, or a general court-martial, the equivalent of felony court.

Maj. Wendell said at the hearing that the case centered on the “tension between First Amendment rights and your obligations as a military officer.” Active-duty service members face strict limitations on their ability to publicly dissent or participate in overtly political causes while in uniform. Even so, prosecutions for “contempt toward officials” under Article 88 are exceptionally rare.

Only two convictions under that article have taken place since the Uniform Code of Military Justice went into effect in 1951, said Daniel Maurer, a retired Army Lieutenant Colonel and Judge Advocate who is now an associate professor of law at Ohio Northern University. The first was Lt. Henry Howe, who was convicted following his participation in a 1965 anti-Vietnam War protest during which he carried a sign calling Lyndon B. Johnson’s actions fascist.

The second was Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller, who was an active-duty Marine in 2021 when he posted a series of social media videos, some in uniform, lambasting the Biden administration’s handling of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan. Lt. Col. Scheller’s case played out in a special court-martial. He resigned from the Marines and as part of a plea deal, he pleaded guilty to multiple charges, received a reprimand letter and forfeited $5,000 in pay.

Those social media videos drew praise from Pete Hegseth, and Lt. Col. Scheller became a senior adviser in the Pentagon after Mr. Hegseth became defense secretary.

Maj. Watson’s defense team leaned heavily on the handling of Lt. Col. Scheller’s case during the hearing on Friday, arguing that with it, the government had set a precedent for such prosecutions and that Lt. Col. Scheller’s violations were far more grave — and his charges more numerous — than Maj. Watson’s.

“Can this prosecution be squared with the evenhanded administration of justice?” Mr. Mutimer asked of Maj. Watson’s case, later adding that “what he did, in the end, was speak.”
